The paper presents a compelling solution to the challenging problem of few-shot non-rigid point cloud registration (N-PCR). The core contribution—UniRiT, a simple two-stage MLP-based framework that separates rigid and non-rigid alignment—is supported by striking empirical results. Most notably, the method achieves near-perfect alignment on a 9-organ benchmark (2.16 mm RMSE) and demonstrates a massive, previously unexplored leap in zero-shot generalization to small bowel data (6.65 mm RMSE vs. >80 mm for all baselines). This finding fundamentally challenges the prevailing assumption that existing methods are capable of cross-organ few-shot transfer, highlighting the brittleness of current approaches and the necessity of the explicit decomposition proposed.

The strength of the paper lies in the robustness of these positive findings. The ablation studies effectively isolate the efficacy of the two-stage architecture, proving that the rigid pre-alignment is not just an architectural detail but a critical factor for performance. The simplicity and efficiency of the method (no transformers/attention, low FLOPs) further enhance its appeal for practical deployment.

However, the paper requires significant attention to technical rigor and transparency before publication. The most critical flaw is the lack of training details for the eight baseline methods. Comparing against baselines that seemingly collapse (yielding near-random alignment) without stating their optimization settings (LR, optimizer, epochs) raises concerns that the dramatic performance gap might be an artifact of poor baseline configuration rather than a genuine architectural superiority. This must be rectified. This distinction must be clearer to reviewers and readers to manage expectations regarding intra-operative applicability. Finally, a missing introduction to the "Livermatch" baseline and unreported hyperparameters hinder reproducibility.

Despite these issues, the scientific contribution is significant. The discovery that a simple two-stage decomposition allows for zero-shot generalization across organs where all prior learning-based methods fail is a high-impact finding. The weaknesses are largely related to experimental reporting, dataset characterization, and consistency of narrative, none of which invalidate the core empirical discoveries.
